title: AI Boom Forces Massive Investment in Power Grids Worldwide

body: Thanksgiving Gas Prices Could Break a Record Despite Recent Plunge What I Cover Irina Slav has been writing about global energy markets since 2007, covering the oil and gas industry, energy security, commodities, and the… The information technology industry is driving massive growth in global electricity demand, which is set to rise by more than 10,000 TWh over the next ten years. For this electricity to reach demand hubs, grids around the world will need urgent upgrades. In its World Energy Outlook released this week, the International Energy Agency once again joined the growing chorus of forecasters warning that data centers are becoming a major drain on electricity supply. Some of these warnings and community opposition to new facilities that may bring their electricity bills higher helped tip the midterm scales in Democrats’ favor. Others are casting doubts about the AI revolution's potential for success if data center operators cannot secure enough electricity for all their planned facilities. The IEA noted the importance of keeping electricity affordable as pro-transition governments try to boost the share of electricity in final energy consumption. “Successful electrification means keeping electricity available and affordable, putting the emphasis on effective use and expansion of grids, and greater operational flexibility in power systems,” the International Energy Agency wrote in the executive summary of its report. It then went on to add that while AI is widely expected to help with things like energy efficiency and grid optimization, “for the moment, surging demand from data centres is amplifying strains in some markets and supply chains.” The financial side of the energy problem with data centers is the most serious one. Net-zero ambitions already required massive spend on new transmission lines before the AI craze began. Now, the tab is just going to go higher as data centers join other demand centers that need to be supplied with reliable, hopefully low-carbon electricity, per the IEA’s and net-zero governments’ agenda. Meanwhile, as it emerges that data center operators tend to split the grid connection bill generously with nearby residents, opposition is likely to grow as well. Related: China’s Oil Imports from Persian Gulf Jump to Wartime High A study from Cornell University this month revealed that wholesale prices for electricity across four regions in the U.S. rose because of demand from data centers. However, the study also found that these data centers’ operators only paid for 38% of the infrastructure costs related to their facilities’ connection to and use of the grid. The remainder fell on local communities. In money terms, data center operators paid $3.12 billion, and households paid $5.13 billion. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that there were some 58 GW in new data centers under construction across the United States, citing data from Cleanview. That total represented 577 locations, whose demand for electricity the WSJ compared to six times the electricity demand of New York City at its peak. A fifth of that total is being built in Texas--but Texas just got a change of the guard, and the newcomers are not big fans of data centers. “We need an immediate moratorium on data centers to last until the legislature can meet to put in place real protections so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities,” Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s campaign website said before the election. On that, she was in agreement with predecessor Greg Abbott, who earlier this year banned new data center approvals to investigate whether they were having a negative impact on energy prices and other issues. Whether the data center building boom slows or not, there is already plenty of new demand for electricity coming from these facilities and, in countries run by strong pro-transition politicians, the drive to replace baseload electricity with wind and solar continues

Brent crude futures rose to $92.57 per barrel and WTI crude futures rose to $83.41 per barrel on November 20, 2026. Oil prices gained on global commodity markets amid rising concern about supply disruptions. Crude oil prices feed into fuel costs and broader energy markets, so supply-risk developments in key producing regions carry global implications. Analysts attributed the rise to Houthi missile attacks on Riyadh and tanker incidents in the Strait of Hormuz. Brent January 2027 futures on London's ICE exchange rose $0.59 (0.64%) to $92.57 per barrel, while WTI January 2027 futures on NYMEX gained $0.97 (1.18%) to $83.41 per barrel. The source does not quantify any actual volume of supply lost to the reported incidents. Oil prices rose on November 20, 2026, after Houthi forces launched missile attacks on Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, and incidents involving oil tankers occurred in the Strait of Hormuz. Analysts linked the gain to growing risks of supply disruption, while expectations that OPEC+ countries will maintain production restrictions also supported prices. The rally reflects expectations that OPEC+ will keep its production restrictions in place, a policy that has tended to tighten crude supply and support prices. Geopolitical risk in the Middle East now adds to that supply-side backdrop. Crude price moves of this size tend to pass through to fuel prices at the pump and to energy costs for households and businesses over time. Readers with exposure to fuel budgets may see the effect as supply-risk premiums shift. title: India's GDP Growth Draws Global Attention as Trump Cites Economic Success to Criticise US Fed - Khalsa Vox
body: India's strong economic growth has found a prominent mention in American political discourse, with US President Donald Trump highlighting the country's 7 per cent GDP expansion while criticising the Federal Reserve's interest rate policies. Speaking at a White House press conference on Friday, November 20, Trump pointed to India's economic performance as an example of how favourable borrowing conditions could support growth. His remarks placed India's economic momentum at the centre of a debate over US monetary policy. "If you look at India, they have low interest rates, and they have a 7 per cent GDP," Trump said, contrasting the Indian economy with the United States. The American President argued that the US could achieve significantly higher growth if its central bank reduced borrowing costs. He suggested that American GDP growth could potentially reach 15 to 20 per cent, although such figures represented his own projections rather than established economic forecasts. Trump also accused the Federal Reserve of being politically influenced, claiming that interest rates remained unnecessarily high despite positive economic indicators. For India, the comparison marks a notable moment of international recognition, with the world's largest economy looking towards India's growth performance during a discussion about its own economic prospects. India has remained among the fastest-growing major economies, supported by domestic economic activity and its expanding presence in global markets. Its growth trajectory has attracted international attention as major economies navigate inflationary pressures, uncertain trade conditions and changing monetary policies. Trump's reference is particularly significant because India was presented as a positive economic comparison rather than merely as an emerging market. The remarks underscore the growing visibility of Indian economic performance in global policy discussions. However, differences between the two economies remain substantial. Interest rate decisions depend on inflation, employment conditions, financial stability and other domestic factors. Lower borrowing costs alone do not guarantee faster economic growth. The Federal Reserve continues to face inflationary pressures, with US annual personal consumption expenditures inflation reportedly reaching 3.6 per cent in September, above its 2 per cent target. Nevertheless, the White House remarks have brought renewed attention to India's economic trajectory. As India strengthens its position in the international economic landscape, Trump's invocation of its growth rate reflects how the country's performance is increasingly becoming part of conversations about global competitiveness and economic policymaking. The comparison also reinforces India's rising profile as a major economy whose growth figures command attention beyond its borders.

title: US President Trump lauds India’s economic growth & low interest rates - The Indian Awaaz
body: US President Donald Trump has praised India’s low interest rates and strong economic growth. He cited India as an example while criticising the US Federal Reserve for damaging the American economy by keeping interest rates high despite strong economic performance. Mr Trump made the comparison at a news conference in Washington last night after returning from a four-day visit to Asia. Referring to India’s economic growth of around seven per cent, President Trump argued that the US economy, currently growing at around four per cent, could expand by 14 to 20 per cent if the Federal Reserve lowered borrowing costs instead of keeping interest rates high. He also said that the United States should be able to borrow money at lower interest rates than any other country. Mr Trump accused the Federal Reserve of taking a political approach to monetary policy and keeping borrowing costs high despite strong economic indicators. The US President further claimed that a 1 percentage point cut in interest rates could save the country 650 billion dollars in debt payments. He also highlighted rising investments in manufacturing, saying factory activity had expanded for ten consecutive months and investment in new equipment had increased by 21 per cent this year. Mr Trump credited his tariff policies with encouraging companies such as Audi and Toyota to invest in manufacturing in the United States. He also pointed to falling oil and petrol prices as signs of economic improvement. He said future petrol prices could depend, in part, on a possible agreement between the United States and Iran. The US Federal Reserve determines interest rates based on economic conditions, particularly inflation and employment, with the twin objectives of maintaining price stability and supporting maximum employment.

title: Nvidia Stock: 5 Reasons the AI Trade Has Only Begun - I/O Fund
body: This week, Nvidia dispelled fears of the AI trade slowing with one simple number; fiscal 2028 revenue growth is guided to be 75% up from 70% despite a higher FY27 revenue base. Vera Rubin generated $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments, which is Nvidia’s fastest ramp ever. The Q4 guide is softer than it appears as it includes an extra week. If we adjust to a 13-week quarter, it works out to $121 billion or roughly 4% sequential growth after three quarters of 20% sequential growth. The guide excludes $2.4 billion in licensed Hopper sales to China that contributed to Q3. Don’t sweat it, though; we’ve been here before. When Nvidia transitions between product generations, the market typically panics as it reads the lull as a permanent slowdown. In fact, some of my very best AI entries have occurred during the pause between generations. As of now, Rubin’s first quarter is nearly double Blackwell’s at $20 billion compared to $11 billion, respectively. Management also stated the ramp is “off to an extraordinary start. During the Blackwell transition, sequential growth slowed to 12% in each of the first two quarters of the ramp, then to 6% in Q2 when H20 sales from China went to zero . After that, sales re-accelerated to 22% and 19% QoQ. Margins are the weaker part of the story, but you’d have to be living under a rock not to expect memory costs to weigh on profitability . Gross margin is expected to fall from 74.9% to 71%-72% in Q4, which the CFO said was a bottom with margins expected to return to 72%-73%. Now that we’ve gotten some of the obligatory earnings coverage out of the way, let’s talk about what’s really on everyone’s minds – is the AI trade over? Or perhaps equally concerning, is AI slowing to the point the glory years are behind us? Before we discuss the facts, I would encourage investors to pay close attention to who is spreading fear, uncertainty and doubt when the underlying fundamentals remain strong. Valid concerns are worth considering, but investors should deeply question why the concerns are brought up after a steep selloff rather than before it. Psychology is a major component of successful investing, and there is not a more important time to protect your mindset than when stock prices are at a multi-year low. Case in point, you’d have to go back at least 10 years to find Nvidia trading this low; therefore, it’s reasonable that many years go by until investors see some of these valuations again. With that in mind, below are five reasons we believe the current panic may be presenting investors with a rare buying opportunity, rather than signaling the end of the AI trade. The defining characteristic of the AI infrastructure cycle continues to be demand greatly exceeding supply. AI suppliers are building against contracted demand, which is distinguished from previous tech bubbles when suppliers were building on speculative demand. For example, SK Hynix has stated they are effectively sold out through 2029. Nvidia’s supply-related commitments rose to $390 billion, which reflects the sheer scale of supply chain expansion as this is up 3X over two quarters, given commitments were $119 billion in the April quarter. Another indication of the strong demand from Nvidia’s report was the statement that cloud industry backlog increased from $2 trillion to $2.5 trillion. The 25% sequential increase reinforces a significant step-up in cloud customers’ future demand, supported by multiyear visibility. Here is what was stated on the earnings call by CFO Collette Kress: “Our hyperscale customers’ cloud revenue growth accelerated for the sixth consecutive quarter. Cloud industry backlog now sits at $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago, underscoring the significant multi-year opportunity ahead of our partners and of NVIDIA.” Nvidia reported that token prices have declined 60% since May, yet rather than weaken demand for compute, lower prices are helping to accelerate consumption.
